notes: Slot 4 = Communist Party of Turkmenistan under Gapurov (First Secretary since Dec 1969). Real institutions used where they existed: Radio Liberty Turkmen desk (0), Writers' Union (1), trade unions (3), Komsomol (5, rather than MD's slot-6 successor body), republican KGB (7, high-popularity security slot), SADUM's Turkmen qaziyat (10), Council of Ministers (13), Desert Institute (17). Slot 6 = Moscow-installed hardline centralists. Shia slots use the Kopetdag Kurds and the Persian/Azerbaijani community. No MD TRK sprite depicts a 1970 organization, so all icons are null.

0.name: Azatlyk Radiosy
0.text:
The Turkmen desk of Radio Liberty broadcasts into the republic from Munich. Founded in the early 1950s and financed from Washington, it is staffed by émigrés, some of them former wartime legionnaires, others refugees who crossed the Iranian and Afghan frontiers. Soviet jammers cover Central Asia, yet shortwave sets in Ashgabat, Mary and the oases still catch its news, poetry and religious programmes.

Its line is uncompromising anti-communism: it exposes Russification, the purges and the destruction of the 1930s, and promises Turkmens national sovereignty under Western protection. Its listeners are few and scattered among older villagers and curious students, but in a closed republic a foreign voice speaking fluent Turkmen carries weight far beyond its numbers.

1.name: Türkmenistan SSR-iniň Ýazyjylar Soýuzy
1.english: Union of Writers of the Turkmen SSR
1.text:
The Union of Writers of the Turkmen SSR is the republic's official literary body and the guardian of its printed language. Its patriarch is Berdi Kerbabaýew, author of the revolutionary novel ‘Aýgytly ädim’ and of ‘Nebitdag’, and around him gather the poets, novelists and critics who fill Ashgabat's journals and publishing houses.

Loyal to Moscow on paper, the union nurses a cautious cultural conservatism: it defends Turkmen against creeping Russian in schools and offices, champions the classical poet Magtymguly and the Görogly epic, and resists attempts to erase the pre-revolutionary heritage. It has no ministries and no guns, but it shapes how Turkmens see themselves, and the party needs its pens.

2.name: Türkmenfilmiň täze tolkuny
2.text:
The young directors and cameramen of the Turkmenfilm studio in Ashgabat have become the boldest artistic voice in the republic. Bulat Mansurov's ‘The Contest’ and ‘Quenching the Thirst’, adapted from Yuri Trifonov's novel about the builders of the Karakum Canal, and the striking camerawork of Khodjakuli Narliev have won Turkmen cinema attention far beyond Central Asia.

The circle stands for artistic freedom and honest portrayals of village life, old customs and the human cost of Soviet modernisation. It is not anti-Soviet, yet its films test the limits of censorship, and its members admire Italian and French cinema. Its leverage is prestige: festival prizes and all-Union acclaim make it hard for Ashgabat's ideologists to silence.

3.name: Türkmenistanyň Kärdeşler Arkalaşyklarynyň Respublikan Soweti
3.english: Turkmen Republican Council of Trade Unions
3.text:
The Turkmen Republican Council of Trade Unions organises the oilmen of Nebitdag and Çeleken, the textile workers of Ashgabat, the dockers of Krasnovodsk and the hundreds of thousands employed on state farms and construction sites. Like every Soviet union body it answers to the party, administering social insurance, sanatoria, housing queues and holiday vouchers rather than leading strikes.

Within those limits it voices a cautious social reformism: higher wages and shorter shifts in the scorching summer, better housing in the canal settlements, more consumer goods and the bonuses promised by the Kosygin reforms. Its strength lies in sheer membership and control of welfare funds, which make it the regime's main channel to the working class.

4.name: Türkmenistanyň Kommunistik Partiýasy
4.text:
The Communist Party of Turkmenistan is the republican branch of the CPSU and the only legal party in the Turkmen SSR. In December 1969 Muhammetnazar Gapurov, until then chairman of the republic's Council of Ministers, replaced Balysh Ovezov as First Secretary, and he is now installing his own cadres in Ashgabat and the district committees.

The party follows Brezhnev's line of stability and cadre security and pledges unconditional loyalty to Moscow. Its priorities are cotton, the extension of the Karakum Canal and the exploitation of newly discovered gas fields in the desert. Its power is total: it appoints every director, editor and kolkhoz chairman, and its patronage reaches deep into the tribal networks of the Ahal, Mary, Çärjew and Daşhowuz oases.

5.name: Türkmenistanyň Leninçi Kommunistik Ýaşlar Soýuzy
5.english: Leninist Communist Youth Union of Turkmenistan
5.text:
The Leninist Communist Youth Union of Turkmenistan is the party's youth organisation, enrolling most students, young workers and conscripts. It sends shock brigades to the Karakum Canal, the new gas fields and the cotton harvest, and runs the newspapers, clubs and summer camps through which ambitious young Turkmens begin their careers.

Beneath the official ritual lives a genuine radical impulse: impatient activists who take the revolution literally, denounce bribe-taking officials, bride-price and the seclusion of girls, and demand faster industrialisation and promotion on merit. Firmly pro-Soviet, it draws its leverage from numbers and enthusiasm, and from the fact that tomorrow's party secretaries are today's Komsomol organisers.

6.name: Moskwanyň gözi
6.text:
Moscow's Eye is the hardline centralist bloc in the republican apparatus, gathered around the Russian second secretary of the Central Committee, the Slavic heads of key departments and veteran cadres formed under Stalin. Since the 1920s Moscow has placed its own men beside every Turkmen leader to watch over appointments, security and the cotton plan.

The bloc distrusts native cadres and their tribal loyalties, demands stricter ideological discipline and more Russian-language schooling, and wants writers and historians purged of ‘national narrowness’. It looks for protection to the conservative wing of the Central Committee in Moscow. Its leverage is control of personnel files and a direct line to the Kremlin that can end any local career overnight.

7.name: Türkmenistan SSR-iniň Döwlet Howpsuzlyk Komiteti
7.english: Committee for State Security of the Turkmen SSR
7.text:
The Committee for State Security of the Turkmen SSR is the republican arm of the KGB, headquartered in Ashgabat. Through the Border Troops it guards the long frontier with Iran and Afghanistan, and its officers watch émigré contacts, listeners to foreign radio and unregistered mullahs while keeping files on every writer and official of note.

Its creed is the security state: vigilance against bourgeois nationalism, pan-Turkism and pan-Islamism, and absolute loyalty to the Soviet Union against Western subversion. It answers to Moscow before Ashgabat, which makes it both the party's shield and its potential rival. Its leverage lies in surveillance, informers and the power to turn any rumour into a career-ending case.

8.name: Kurdên Kopetdagê
8.text:
The Kurds of the Kopetdag are Kurmanji-speaking Shia whose ancestors were settled on the Khorasan frontier by the Persian shahs to guard it against Turkmen raids. Their villages in the foothills near Ashgabat now lie inside the Turkmen SSR, cut off from kinsmen in Quchan and Bojnurd since the border was sealed in the 1930s.

Their faith survives in households rather than mosques: Muharram mourning, vows at local shrines and the longing for pilgrimage to Imam Reza in Mashhad, a few hours away across the frontier. Moderate and communal, they seek tolerance for their rites and contact with relatives in Iran, not confrontation with the state. Their leverage is cohesion and a reputation as dependable kolkhoz workers and herdsmen.

9.name: Azadaran-e Eshqabad
9.text:
The Mourners of Ashgabat are clandestine Muharram circles among the Persian and Azerbaijani Shia of Ashgabat and Krasnovodsk, survivors of a once-thriving Iranian merchant community that was largely deported to Iran at the end of the 1930s. With no Shia mosque open to them, they gather in private homes to recite the passion of Imam Husayn.

Their outlook is militant traditionalism: they reject the state's atheism outright, regard the official Muslim board as Sunni and compromised, and look for guidance to the seminaries of Mashhad, where young clerics preach that Islam must rule rather than retreat. Their numbers are tiny, but their leverage lies in secrecy, family loyalty and sermons and books smuggled across the frontier.

10.name: Türkmenistanyň Kazyýaty
10.text:
The Qaziyat of Turkmenistan is the republican office of the Spiritual Administration of the Muslims of Central Asia and Kazakhstan, the state-approved Muslim board seated in Tashkent under Mufti Ziyauddin Babakhanov. Its qazi supervises the handful of registered mosques in the republic and the few imams licensed to lead prayers, marry couples and bury the dead.

It preaches an Islam reconciled with Soviet power: loyalty to the state, support for Soviet peace diplomacy in the Muslim world and a scripturalist line that condemns shrine cults, ishan veneration and costly feasts as superstition. Its mosques are nearly empty, but its leverage rests on being the only Muslim voice the state permits to speak in public.

11.name: Gazawatçylar
11.text:
The Ghazawat Fighters are a scattered underground of unlicensed mullahs, sons of Basmachi fighters and young men taught in secret hujra schools in the Daşhowuz and Çärjew oases. They keep alive the memory of the armed resistance of the 1920s and 1930s and stay in touch, through traders and shepherds, with Turkmen exiles in northern Afghanistan.

Their goal is a Muslim Turkestan won by holy war and ruled by sharia under a caliph, free of Moscow and of every atheist party. They brand the official mufti a servant of unbelief and see both superpowers as enemies of Islam. They have no organisation worth the name, but the KGB fears that hardship, revival or war on the border could turn whispers into insurrection.

12.name: Mukaddes öwlatlar
12.text:
The Holy Lineages are the Turkmen öwlat tribes, the Hoja, Seyit, Şyh, Magtym and Ata, who claim descent from the Prophet, the first caliphs or Sufi saints, together with the ishan families who once led the Naqshbandi brotherhoods. Stripped of their endowments and many shrines in the 1930s, they survive within the kolkhozes as respected families and keepers of graves.

They practise a gentle, communal Islam: pilgrimage to holy tombs, blessings at weddings and circumcisions, healing prayers and Qur'an lessons at home. They avoid open politics and accommodate Soviet rule, but want faith to keep its place in family and village life. Their leverage is moral authority, for no feast, funeral or marriage is complete without them.

13.name: Türkmenistan SSR-iniň Ministrler Soweti
13.english: Council of Ministers of the Turkmen SSR
13.text:
The Council of Ministers of the Turkmen SSR is the republic's government, directing the ministries, the State Planning Committee and the economic administration from Ashgabat. Since Gapurov moved from its chairmanship to the party leadership in December 1969, its engineers, economists and planners carry the daily burden of the five-year plan.

Its outlook is technocratic rather than ideological: it bargains with Moscow's Gosplan over investment, pushes irrigation, gas, oil and light industry, and prefers orderly targets to campaigns. It is part of the Soviet system, yet it guards republican interests in every budget negotiation. Its leverage lies in expertise and control over the flow of resources, supplies and appointments.

14.name: Ýaşulular maslahaty
14.text:
The Council of Elders is the informal authority of the white-bearded ýaşulular who still lead the Teke, Ýomut, Ärsary, Salyr and Saryk tribes behind the façade of the collective farms. Collectivisation broke their herds and holdings, yet tribe and lineage still decide marriages, disputes, water shares and even who becomes kolkhoz chairman or district secretary.

They are conservatives of a quiet, rural kind: they defend bride-price, family honour, customary law and the authority of age, and distrust Russian newcomers and urban radicals alike. Neither pro-Western nor truly Soviet, they know how to live with whoever controls the canals. Their leverage is the village itself, which no outsider can govern without their consent.

15.name: Nebitdag topary
15.text:
The Nebitdag Group is the network of oil and gas managers centred on the Caspian fields of Nebitdag and Çeleken and the growing gas industry of the Karakum. Its directors, geologists and drilling chiefs run enterprises subordinated directly to all-Union ministries in Moscow, with budgets, housing and supplies far larger than any republican body commands.

They want more investment, more autonomy for enterprises and a larger share of hydrocarbon wealth kept in Turkmenistan, and see themselves as the republic's real modernisers. Politically they are loyal technocrats with privileged access to Moscow's ministers. Their leverage is economic: whoever controls the wells, pipelines and supply depots controls the most valuable assets in the republic.

16.name: Tolkuçka söwdagärleri
16.text:
The Tolkuchka Traders are the sellers, middlemen and speculators of Ashgabat's great weekend market on the edge of the desert, linked to private-plot farmers, carpet weavers and the shadow workshops that produce what the planned economy cannot. Officially tolerated as a kolkhoz market, Tolkuchka is in practice the freest economic space in the republic.

Its people want the right to buy, sell and produce for profit: larger private plots, free trade in carpets, livestock and melons, and fewer price controls and police raids. They have no ideology beyond self-reliance and care for neither bloc except as a source of goods. Their leverage is indispensability, for officials, officers and party families all shop and bargain there.

17.name: Türkmenistan SSR Ylymlar Akademiýasynyň Çöller Instituty
17.english: Desert Institute of the Turkmen Academy of Sciences
17.native_full: Türkmenistan SSR Ylymlar Akademiýasynyň Çöller Instituty
17.text:
The Desert Institute of the Turkmen Academy of Sciences, founded in 1962 and directed by Agajan Babaýew, is the Soviet Union's leading centre for the study of arid lands. Its scientists work at the Repetek reserve, in the sands of the Karakum and along the new canal, mapping dunes, pastures, groundwater and the spread of salt.

From that research grows an early conservationism: warnings against salinisation and waterlogging along the Karakum Canal, overgrazing of desert pastures and the felling of saxaul woods, and calls for more reserves and careful irrigation. It does not challenge the party, but it insists that the desert has limits. Its leverage is expertise and the respect of all-Union planners who need its data.

18.name: Ak altyn başlyklary
18.text:
The White Gold Chairmen are the heads of the great cotton kolkhozes and state farms of the Murgap, Tejen and Amyderýa oases, many of them decorated Heroes of Socialist Labour. They command land, water, machinery and thousands of collective farmers, and the annual cotton plan, the republic's chief obligation to the Union, depends on them.

They stand for an agrarian socialism of the countryside: higher purchase prices for cotton, more irrigation, rural schools, clinics and electrification, and respect for the village against urban planners. Loyal to the Soviet order that made them, they bargain hard within it. Their leverage lies in the harvest itself, for no first secretary survives a failed cotton plan.

19.name: Atabaýewiň ýoly
19.text:
Atabaýew's Path is the national-communist outlook of Turkmen party intellectuals who honour Kaýgysyz Atabaýew and Nedirbaý Aýtakow, the founders of Soviet Turkmenistan, both shot in 1938 and rehabilitated after Stalin's death. In history institutes, party schools and newspaper offices their legacy is studied and quietly invoked.

Its adherents are Marxists who want a Turkmen road to socialism: wider republican autonomy within the Union, native cadres in leading posts, Turkmen as a language of administration and an honest history of the 1920s. They reject both Moscow's centralism and Western capitalism. Their leverage lies in the native intelligentsia and party ranks, where national pride and communist conviction often go together.

20.name: Gökdepe ýady
20.text:
The Memory of Gökdepe is a nationalist mood among Teke villagers, students and intellectuals that keeps alive the siege of 1881, when Russian troops stormed the fortress of Gökdepe and cut down its defenders and fleeing families. Official history praises the progressive significance of the Russian conquest, but the story survives in the families and laments of the Ahal oasis.

Its adherents resent Russian settlers, privileges for Slavic cadres and the dominance of Russian in towns and offices, and want Turkmens to be masters in their own land. They have no organisation, programme or foreign patron and trust neither Moscow nor the West. Their leverage is emotional: one spark of injustice could turn private grievance into crowds in the streets.

21.name: Türküstan legionerleri
21.text:
The Turkestan Legionnaires are the survivors of the Turkmen battalions raised by the Wehrmacht from Soviet prisoners of war during the Second World War. Some live in exile in West Germany and Turkey; others were repatriated, served long sentences in the camps and returned in silence to their villages, branded as traitors.

Their die-hards still dream of a Greater Turkestan from the Caspian to Xinjiang, an authoritarian Turkic state purged of Russians and communists, and pass the pan-Turkic, anti-Bolshevik slogans of the war years to a few younger listeners. Hated by the state and few in number, they matter through networks of exiles and returnees that tie the republic to an older, darker nationalism.

22.name: Guşgy garnizony
22.text:
The Kushka Garrison stands for the Soviet officer corps in the Turkmen SSR, from the frontier fortress at Kushka, the southernmost point of the Union, to the motor-rifle units and air bases around Ashgabat and Mary. Its forces belong to the Turkestan Military District in Tashkent, and its officers are overwhelmingly Russian and Ukrainian.

Its creed is military order: security on the Iranian and Afghan borders, readiness for war in the south and contempt for disorder, nationalism and tribal politics. It is unconditionally loyal to Moscow, but in a crisis its commanders would be the decisive force in the republic. Its leverage is simple: the guns, the frontier and the right to declare that order has broken down.

23.name: Jüneýit hanyň mirasdarlary
23.text:
The Heirs of Junaid Khan are the kinsmen and followers of the Ýomut chieftain who made himself master of Khiva in 1918 and fought Soviet power until he fled across the border; he died in exile in Herat in 1938. His clans live among the Turkmen refugees of northern Afghanistan and Iran, while in the Daşhowuz oasis his name is still spoken with awe.

They cherish the idea of a Turkmen khanate under a strong ruler of noble lineage, with tribal councils and Islamic law. They reject Soviet rule entirely and hope for help from Kabul or Tehran. Their leverage is the legend itself: in a moment of collapse, a khan's name could still rally the Ýomut tribes.
